questions.question: Explain the differences between `var`, `let`, and `const`. When can a `const` value still change?
questions.answer: `var` is function-scoped, hoisted and initialized to `undefined`, can be redeclared or reassigned. `let` is block-scoped, hoisted but in the TDZ until initialized, reassignable but not redeclarable. `const` is block-scoped, in the TDZ, must be initialized at declaration, and cannot be reassigned or redeclared. A `const` binding to an object or array can still be mutated (`user.name = "Asha"`, `arr.push(1)`); only rebinding the name is forbidden.
key_points: var = function scope, let/const = block scope
let reassignable, const not reassignable
const does not make objects immutable
const must be initialized at declaration

questions.question: What is hoisting, and how does the temporal dead zone differ from `var`'s `undefined`?
questions.answer: Hoisting is the engine registering declarations before execution. `var` is registered and initialized to `undefined`, so reading it early gives `undefined`. `let`/`const` are registered but left uninitialized; the period before initialization is the temporal dead zone, so reading them throws `ReferenceError`. Function declarations are fully hoisted and callable before their line; function expressions only hoist their variable binding.
key_points: Hoisting moves declarations, not assignments
var reads as undefined
let/const throw in the TDZ
Function declarations are fully hoisted; expressions are not

questions.question: What does this print, and why? `let ok = true; { console.log(typeof ok); let ok = false; }`
questions.answer: It throws `ReferenceError: Cannot access 'ok' before initialization`. The inner `let ok` shadows the outer one for the entire block, and `typeof` is not magic: it is safe for a completely undeclared name but throws for a `let`/`const` binding that is still in its temporal dead zone.
key_points: Inner let shadows the outer binding
TDZ spans the whole block before initialization
typeof throws for TDZ names
typeof only saves you for undeclared names

questions.question: True or false: `const user = { name: "Kakade" }; user.name = "Asha";` throws because `user` is const.
questions.answer: False. It succeeds and `user.name` becomes `"Asha"`. `const` prevents reassigning the binding (`user = {}` throws `TypeError`), not mutating the object it points to. To make the object itself immutable you need `Object.freeze(user)`.
key_points: const protects the binding, not the value
Object mutation is allowed
Reassignment throws TypeError
Object.freeze gives shallow immutability

questions.question: What is shadowing, and why is `let name = "Kakade"; { var name = "Asha"; }` a syntax error while `let name = "Kakade"; { let name = "Asha"; }` is fine?
questions.answer: Shadowing is an inner binding hiding an outer one. The second version is fine because the inner `let` creates a separate block-scoped binding. The `var` version is a SyntaxError: `var` is not block-scoped, so it tries to declare `name` in the function/global scope where a `let name` already exists, which is an illegal redeclaration. The whole script fails at parse time.
key_points: Shadowing = inner scope hides outer name
let can shadow let legally
var cannot cross an existing let/const binding
It is a parse-time SyntaxError, not catchable
